rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> greenhouse lysimeter experiments (six lysimeters, three replicates per treatment) with and without sweet corn plus Hydrus-2d simulations on Kidman sandy loam. Q2: Abstract and Results 'Distribution of Plant-Available Phosphorus <U+2013> No Uptake' / Fig. 5 <U+2013> continuous drip fertigation gave 20<U+2013>25% higher bicarbonate-extractable P around the emitter than 2-d pulsed application; Conclusion states continuous application gave greater P mobility and higher soil solution P around emitters than intermittent. Q3: 'Comparison of Simulation and Lysimeter Results' <U+2013> both the Hydrus-2d simulation (Fig. 4) and the lysimeter soil sampling (Fig. 5) show zones of higher available P under continuous relative to intermittent application. Q4: Fig. 3 and Fig. 5, tensiometer monitoring <U+2013> soil water content distribution was modeled and measured; soil around emitters was wetter under continuous treatment, and the no-surfacing/stable wetting pattern is used to explain the P distribution. Q8: 'Comparison of Simulation and Lysimeter Results' <U+2013> modeled (soluble) and measured (bicarbonate-extractable) P not directly comparable; idealized soil representation ignoring variability and preferential flow; Langmuir isotherm inadequate for P transport; 'Uptake' section <U+2013> differences in soil P distribution were not evident when corn was grown and irrigation P was low.
rows.notes: Single soil (Kidman sandy loam), single crop, single greenhouse site, lysimeter scale only. The finding that the soil-P effect disappeared with a crop and low P concentration is reported as a variation, not stated as a requirement, so Q7 is no. Standard deviations are given only for biomass and plant tissue P (Figs. 6 and 8), not for the soil extractable P distribution (Fig. 5 isocharts of averages), so Q9 is no. The simulation was only qualitatively compared with measurements; the triangulation judgement rests on model plus lysimeter sampling pointing the same way.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> own lysimeter experiments (three replicates per fertigation treatment, 42 soil samples per lysimeter) and Hydrus-2d simulations. Q2: Abstract and Results/Fig. 5 <U+2013> extractable (Olsen bicarbonate) P in soil immediately surrounding the point source was 20<U+2013>25% higher under continuous than pulsed drip fertigation in bare soil; continuous treatment showed higher P concentrations and greater downward transport. Q3: 'Comparison of Simulation and Lysimeter Results' <U+2013> simulated soil solution P (Fig. 4) and measured extractable P (Fig. 5) both show zones of higher available P under continuous application. Q4: Figs. 3 and 5 and tensiometers <U+2013> water content distribution modeled and measured; soil around emitters wetter under continuous treatment, surfacing of water under pulsed treatment explains lateral P spread. Q8: 'Comparison of Simulation and Lysimeter Results' <U+2013> model and measured P not directly comparable, idealized soil, Langmuir isotherm inadequate; 'Uptake' section <U+2013> the soil P difference was not evident with a corn crop and low irrigation P (extractable P actually lower under continuous in cropped lysimeters).
rows.notes: Claim matches the abstract result closely. The 20<U+2013>25% figure comes from a single-time snapshot (Day 13) of three replicate lysimeters on one calcareous sandy loam in a greenhouse; no dispersion statistic is reported for the soil extractable P values (only isocharts of averages), so Q9 is no. Effect was not reproduced in the cropped experiment, which the authors report but do not frame as a stated requirement (Q7 no).

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a greenhouse lysimeter plus Hydrus-2d simulation comparison of continuous versus 2-d pulsed drip fertigation on one soil with and without sweet corn; the soil P availability result holds in bare soil but not in the cropped experiment, where the benefit appeared instead as higher plant tissue P and biomass.
